summary: Jon Postel gives three suggestions for detecting messages lost by the network's communications subsystem. The first is for a host to keep a copy of each message until the network says it was delivered, and to resend it with a limit on retries if the network reports an incomplete transmission.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 516 proposes three ways for hosts to notice lost messages: keep copies until delivery is confirmed, number messages so gaps can be detected, or add acknowledgments between hosts. The author says these approaches could be used together.

questions: what are the three lost message detection schemes
subtitle: Three proposals for detecting messages lost by the network communications subsystem.

tldr.problem: The communications subsystem could lose messages, and hosts needed ways to detect the loss.
tldr.mechanism: The memo suggests saving and retransmitting messages, numbering messages to detect gaps, or adding host-to-host acknowledgments.
tldr.outcome: The author calls saving and retransmitting the most immediately practical scheme and says the approaches do not conflict.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 516's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. It is a proposal for detecting message loss in the host communications subsystem.

sections.title: Three Ways to Detect Loss
sections.content: Jonathan Postel offers three suggestions for detecting messages lost by the communications subsystem. The first uses existing concepts and can retransmit a message when it is reported lost. The RFC says the three schemes do not conflict and could be implemented together.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo offers three ways for a host to find out that a message may be missing. They can be considered separately or used together.

sections.title: Save a Copy and Retransmit
sections.content:
After sending a message, a host keeps a copy and waits for the network's response. An RFNM means the host can process the next message. An INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSION response causes the host to retransmit its copy, with a finite limit to prevent an endless loop. A DESTINATION DEAD response marks the destination down and requires reset commands before communication continues.

Other responses indicate an error in the network or local IMP. The RFC says the host should at least log the error and probably close the conversation. The procedure can be used per host or per link.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a copy until it receives a response. It can resend after an incomplete transmission, but the RFC says retries need a limit.

sections.title: Message Numbers and Host Acknowledgments
sections.content:
The second scheme adds message numbers to the Host-Host header. A receiver compares each number with the expected value and detects a loss when they differ. The example increments numbers modulo N, with N=256. The memo notes that this approach assumes messages arrive in order and says hosts would need to send either all messages as priority or none as priority.

The third scheme requires acknowledgments from one host to another, similar to the IMP-to-IMP method. The author says this would be a serious change to current protocols and needs further study. If a missing message is not recovered, the memo suggests closing the conversation because loss may be tolerable in an interactive exchange but critical in file transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Message numbers reveal gaps, while acknowledgments let the other host confirm receipt. The memo notes that host acknowledgments would require a major protocol change.

items.title: Save and resend
items.text: Keep a copy until RFNM; retransmit on INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSION.

items.title: Number messages
items.text: Compare the received number with the expected number.

items.title: Host acknowledgments
items.text: Require one host to acknowledge messages from the other.
